The Outlet lets water flow downstream with a prescribed flow rate.
It is similar to the Pump, except that water only flows down, by gravity.

When PID controlled, the Outlet must point towards the controlled Basin in terms of links.

# Tables

## Static

```{julia}
# | code-fold: true
include("../../../utils/gen_docs_table.jl")
const OUTLET_RESTRICTIONS = Dict(:flow_rate => "non-negative")
table_from_schema(Ribasim.Schema.Outlet.Static; restrictions = OUTLET_RESTRICTIONS)
```

## Time

This table is the transient form of the `Outlet` table.
With this all parameters can be updated over time. In between the given times the
values are block interpolated (forward fill), and outside the values are constant given by the
nearest time value.
Note that a `node_id` can be either in this table or in the static one, but not both.

```{julia}
# | code-fold: true
table_from_schema(Ribasim.Schema.Outlet.Time; restrictions = OUTLET_RESTRICTIONS)
```

# Equations

The Outlet is very similar to the Pump, but it has an extra [reduction factor](/reference/node/basin.qmd#sec-reduction-factor) for physical constraints:

$$
Q = \phi_\text{level} \, \mathrm{clamp}(\phi_\text{storage} Q_\text{set}, Q_{\min}, Q_{\max})
$$

- $Q$ is the actual Outlet flow rate.
- $Q_\text{set}$ is the Outlet's target `flow_rate`.
- $Q_{\min}$ and $Q_{\max}$ are the Outlet `min_flow_rate` and `max_flow_rate`.
- $\phi_\text{storage}$ is the reduction factor that smoothly reduces flow when the upstream volume is below the equivalent of a water depth of `depth_threshold`.
- $\phi_\text{level}$ is the product of the reduction factors that smoothly reduce flow based on these criteria:
  - The upstream level goes from `downstream_level` + `level_difference_threshold` to `downstream_level`.
  - The upstream level goes from `min_upstream_level` + `level_difference_threshold` to `min_upstream_level`.
  - The downstream level goes from `max_downstream_level` - `level_difference_threshold` to `max_downstream_level`.

For `depth_threshold`, `level_difference_threshold` see [Solver settings](/reference/usage.qmd#sec-solver-settings).

Since $\phi_\text{level}$ is applied after the clamp, `min_flow_rate` is not a strict minimum: the level criteria can still reduce the flow to zero.

# Behavior in allocation

How an Outlet behaves in [allocation](/concept/allocation.qmd) depends on `allocation_controlled` in the [Static](#static) table.

An Outlet that is not allocation-controlled (the default) keeps the flow rate given in its tables or by its control node.
Allocation takes this flow into account, but does not change it.

For an allocation-controlled Outlet, allocation sets the flow rate between `min_flow_rate` and `max_flow_rate`, to bring water to where it is needed.
This flow rate is used until the next intervention time, set by `intervention_interval` in the [allocation settings](/reference/usage.qmd#sec-allocation-settings), and is in [`allocation_control.nc`](/reference/usage.qmd#sec-results).
The simulated flow in `flow.nc` can be lower than this flow rate, for instance when the upstream Basin is almost empty, when the upstream level is not higher than the downstream level, or when `min_upstream_level` or `max_downstream_level` is reached.
An allocation-controlled Outlet needs a finite `max_flow_rate`.
An Outlet that connects the primary network to a secondary network must be allocation-controlled, and a [DiscreteControl](/reference/node/discrete-control.qmd) node can switch allocation control on and off.

A [FlowDemand](/reference/node/flow-demand.qmd) on an Outlet is a minimum flow rate when allocation is not used.
With allocation it is a demand like the others: it is met in the order of its demand priority, so it can get less water than demanded when water is scarce.

With a route priority for Outlet nodes, see [allocation settings](/reference/usage.qmd#sec-allocation-settings), allocation can be made to prefer or avoid routing water through them.
